grades.quote: sleep(&pipe, &pipe->lock) { // in sleep() acquire(&p->lock) release(&pipe->lock) p->state = SLEEPING
grades.reason: Shows the sleep() lock-overlap pattern (condition lock held, then p->lock, process marked SLEEPING) used to avoid lost wake-ups. It touches on the sleeping side but does not compare spinning and sleeping locks under contention.

grades.quote: The waiting threads are organized into a queue, although they continue to run busy-waiting loops, unlike with a scheduler-supported wait queue.
grades.reason: Covers how spinlocks behave under contention: test-and-test-and-set, and queueing spinlocks that still busy-wait. It contrasts them briefly with scheduler-supported wait queues. It is useful for the spinning side and gives only a brief contrast with sleeping.

grades.quote: If multiple processes on different CPUs try to allocate pages at the same time, each will have to wait for its turn by spinning in acquire. Spinning wastes CPU time, since it’s not useful work.
grades.reason: Explains the cost of spinning under lock contention: processes wait by spinning in acquire, which wastes CPU time. It also discusses coarse versus fine-grained locking to reduce contention. It does not directly compare this with sleeping locks.

grades.quote: The basic idea is to have sleep mark the current process as SLEEPING and then call sched to release the CPU; wakeup looks for a process sleeping on the given wait channel and marks it as RUNNABLE.
grades.reason: Describes the sleep/wakeup mechanism, where a process marks itself SLEEPING and releases the CPU instead of spinning. This is auxiliary background for the sleeping side. It makes no explicit comparison with spinlocks under contention.
